## Understanding the problem

You gain 1 point by paying an unmarked enemy's energy (requires currentEnergy ≥ its energy), and you may 'mark' an unmarked enemy to absorb its energy, but only if you already have ≥ 1 point. Maximize points.

Example 1 `[3,2,2], cur=2`: attack a 2-cost enemy (pts 1, energy 0), mark the 3 (energy 3), attack (pts 2, energy 1), mark the other 2 (energy 3), attack (pts 3). Answer 3. Example 2 `[2], cur=10`: five attacks on the lone enemy → 5.

Greedy insight: the cheapest enemy is the most efficient 'attack target' (points per energy), and every other enemy is best used purely as an energy battery. So: keep exactly one copy of the minimum-energy enemy unmarked, mark everything else to bank their energy, then farm the minimum repeatedly.
k: If currentEnergy < min(enemyEnergies), no attack is ever possible (energy only grows via marking, which needs a point) → answer 0.
Optimal play: obtain the first point by attacking a minimum-energy enemy, mark all other enemies to collect their energy, then spend everything attacking the minimum again and again.
Answer = floor((currentEnergy + sum − min) / min) once currentEnergy ≥ min.

a.i: With one min-value enemy kept as the recurring target, total spendable energy is currentEnergy + (sum of all other energies), and each point costs exactly min. The count of affordable attacks is the floor division. Achievability: attack the min once to unlock marking, mark the rest, then continue attacking the min.
a.t: O(n) — one pass for min and sum.

a.i: Simulate the strategy explicitly: sort energies, attack the cheapest whenever affordable; otherwise, if points > 0, mark the largest remaining enemy to refill energy; stop when neither move is possible. This makes the greedy concrete and is easy to defend in an interview, though it does more work than the closed-form.
s: Sort energies ascending; keep pointer i = 0 (cheapest unmarked attack target) and j = n−1 (largest battery).
While true: if currentEnergy ≥ e[i], attack (points++, energy −= e[i]); else if points > 0 and j > i, mark e[j] (energy += e[j], j−−); else break.
a.t: O(n log n) for sorting; the two-pointer loop is O(n).

w:
## Wrap-up

The formula approach is optimal and trivially fast; the simulation is a good fallback if you're unsure of the closed form. Pitfalls: missing the currentEnergy < min ⇒ 0 edge case, and integer overflow of the sum in fixed-width languages (use 64-bit). Follow-up: what if marking also consumed a point, or energies had to be attacked in a fixed order?
